passages.title: The Day Water Had a Name
passages.text:
In the days that followed I learned to spell in this uncomprehending way a great many words, among them pin, hat, cup and a few verbs like sit, stand and walk. But my teacher had been with me several weeks before I understood that everything has a name.

One day, while I was playing with my new doll, Miss Sullivan put my big rag doll into my lap also, spelled "d-o-l-l" and tried to make me understand that "d-o-l-l" applied to both. Earlier in the day we had had a tussle over the words "m-u-g" and "w-a-t-e-r." Miss Sullivan had tried to impress it upon me that "m-u-g" is mug and that "w-a-t-e-r" is water, but I persisted in confounding the two. In despair she had dropped the subject for the time, only to renew it at the first opportunity. I became impatient at her repeated attempts and, seizing the new doll, I dashed it upon the floor. I was keenly delighted when I felt the fragments of the broken doll at my feet. Neither sorrow nor regret followed my passionate outburst. I had not loved the doll. In the still, dark world in which I lived there was no strong sentiment or tenderness. I felt my teacher sweep the fragments to one side of the hearth, and I had a sense of satisfaction that the cause of my discomfort was removed. She brought me my hat, and I knew I was going out into the warm sunshine. This thought, if a wordless sensation may be called a thought, made me hop and skip with pleasure.

We walked down the path to the well-house, attracted by the fragrance of the honeysuckle with which it was covered. Some one was drawing water and my teacher placed my hand under the spout. As the cool stream gushed over one hand she spelled into the other the word water, first slowly, then rapidly. I stood still, my whole attention fixed upon the motions of her fingers. Suddenly I felt a misty consciousness as of something forgotten--a thrill of returning thought; and somehow the mystery of language was revealed to me. I knew then that "w-a-t-e-r" meant the wonderful cool something that was flowing over my hand. That living word awakened my soul, gave it light, hope, joy, set it free! There were barriers still, it is true, but barriers that could in time be swept away.

I left the well-house eager to learn. Everything had a name, and each name gave birth to a new thought. As we returned to the house every object which I touched seemed to quiver with life. That was because I saw everything with the strange, new sight that had come to me. On entering the door I remembered the doll I had broken. I felt my way to the hearth and picked up the pieces. I tried vainly to put them together. Then my eyes filled with tears; for I realized what I had done, and for the first time I felt repentance and sorrow.

I learned a great many new words that day. I do not remember what they all were; but I do know that mother, father, sister, teacher were among them--words that were to make the world blossom for me, "like Aaron's rod, with flowers." It would have been difficult to find a happier child than I was as I lay in my crib at the close of that eventful day and lived over the joys it had brought me, and for the first time longed for a new day to come.
passages.source_note: Public domain: from The Story of My Life by Helen Keller (1903). Straight quotation marks substituted for typographic ones.

questions.stem: According to the first paragraph, how long had the teacher been with the writer before the writer understood that everything has a name?

options.text: A single day
Several weeks
A few hours
Several months
A whole year

questions.explanation: The passage states the teacher 'had been with me several weeks before I understood that everything has a name'.

questions.stem: What does the description of the writer living in a 'still, dark world' most strongly suggest about her before this day?

options.text: She preferred to be alone in quiet rooms
She lived in a house with the curtains always drawn
She was frightened of bright light and loud noise
She was cut off from sound and sight and from the meanings words carry
She had chosen to ignore the people around her

questions.explanation: 'Still' and 'dark' together, with 'no strong sentiment or tenderness', point to a life sealed off from sound, sight and shared meaning, not a literal dark room.

questions.stem: In 'I persisted in confounding the two', what does 'confounding' mean as it is used here?

options.text: Defeating an enemy
Amazing an audience
Building carefully
Explaining clearly
Mixing up or muddling

questions.explanation: She kept 'confounding' mug and water -- she muddled the two together and could not tell them apart.

questions.stem: What made the writer feel 'a sense of satisfaction' after the doll was broken?

options.text: That her teacher praised her cleverness
That she would be given a brand-new doll
That the cause of her discomfort had been removed
That she was allowed to go out early
That the honeysuckle smelled so sweet

questions.explanation: The text says she 'had a sense of satisfaction that the cause of my discomfort was removed'.

questions.stem: Why does the writer describe the broken doll early on and then return to those same pieces near the end of the passage?

options.text: To show, by contrast, how much she has changed once she can feel and understand
To remind the reader which toys she owned as a child
To prove that the doll could be mended if she tried hard enough
To fill space between the two outdoor scenes
To suggest the doll was the most valuable thing she had

questions.explanation: The careless breaking comes before understanding; picking up the pieces 'with tears' afterward measures her change -- the return is deliberate contrast.

questions.stem: In 'every object which I touched seemed to quiver with life', which device is the writer using?

options.text: A rhetorical question
Personification
Alliteration
An exaggeration meant as a joke
A direct quotation

questions.explanation: Ordinary objects are given the living action of 'quiver with life', so lifeless things are described as if alive -- personification.

questions.stem: Why did the teacher spell the word for water 'first slowly, then rapidly' at the pump?

options.text: To test how fast the writer could copy her fingers
To hurry the writer away from the cold stream
To show off how quickly she herself could spell
To make the lesson as difficult as possible
To let the feeling of the water and the spelled word connect in the writer's mind

questions.explanation: Slow then fast, while cool water ran over the hand, was meant to fuse the sensation with the word so its meaning could dawn -- and it did.

questions.stem: When the writer says the living word 'set it free', what is she suggesting about her soul?

options.text: It was allowed to leave the well-house at last
It was let out of a locked room in the house
It was released from being shut in without language
It was excused from any more lessons that day
It was given permission to break more dolls

questions.explanation: The word 'awakened' her soul and 'set it free' -- freed it from the wordless, sealed-off state described earlier, not a literal release.

questions.stem: Which of these events comes at the very end of the passage?

options.text: The writer dashes the doll upon the floor
The writer longs for a new day to come
Water gushes over the writer's hand at the spout
The teacher sweeps the fragments to one side of the hearth
The writer walks down the path to the well-house

questions.explanation: The passage closes with the writer in her crib at the end of the day, longing 'for a new day to come'.

questions.stem: How would you best describe the tone of the sentence beginning 'That living word awakened my soul'?

options.text: Calm and matter-of-fact
Bitter and resentful
Joyful and full of wonder
Puzzled and uncertain
Gently amused

questions.explanation: The rush of 'light, hope, joy' and the exclamation mark give an exultant, wonder-struck tone.

questions.stem: What do the teacher's actions across the passage -- renewing the lesson and guiding the hand under the spout -- suggest about her character?

options.text: She is easily discouraged by small setbacks
She cares more about being obeyed than about teaching
She is careless about how her lessons are arranged
She prefers to let the child work things out alone
She is patient and determined not to give up on her pupil

questions.explanation: After the earlier failure she does not abandon the task but renews it and finds a fresh way at the pump -- patient and persistent.

questions.stem: The writer says she was 'keenly delighted' when she felt the broken pieces at her feet. Which word keeps the strong feeling of 'keenly'?

options.text: Slightly
Politely
Sharply
Doubtfully
Faintly

questions.explanation: 'Keenly' means the delight was sharp and intense; 'sharply' carries the same strength, while 'slightly' and 'faintly' weaken it.

questions.stem: The barriers that 'could in time be swept away' are described as if they were dust or rubbish. What is the effect of this image?

options.text: It makes the obstacles ahead feel removable rather than permanent
It suggests the writer's home needed a good cleaning
It hints that a storm was about to arrive
It shows the writer disliked untidy places
It proves the barriers had already gone completely

questions.explanation: Comparing the barriers to something that can be 'swept away' makes them seem light and clearable, so the difficulties feel temporary, not fixed.

questions.stem: What was the well-house covered with?

options.text: Ivy
Honeysuckle
Roses
Moss
Wild cherry blossom

questions.explanation: The writer walked to the well-house 'attracted by the fragrance of the honeysuckle with which it was covered'.

questions.stem: Which line best shows that the writer felt NO guilt at the moment she broke the doll?

options.text: made me hop and skip with pleasure
I stood still, my whole attention fixed
Then my eyes filled with tears
I left the well-house eager to learn
Neither sorrow nor regret followed my passionate outburst

questions.explanation: The absence of guilt at that moment is stated directly: 'Neither sorrow nor regret followed my passionate outburst'.

questions.stem: In the phrase 'the warm sunshine', what part of speech is the word 'warm'?

options.text: A verb
An adverb
A noun
A pronoun
An adjective

questions.explanation: 'Warm' describes the noun 'sunshine', so it is an adjective.

questions.stem: Why does the writer bother to name 'water' as one of the words she muddled earlier in the day?

options.text: Because 'water' is the very word that later breaks through to her at the pump
Because she disliked drinking from a mug
Because it proves her teacher taught the wrong words at first
Because it explains an argument she had with her mother
Because the mug and the water were both kept in the well-house

questions.explanation: Naming 'water' early is not idle detail: it is the same word that, at the pump, finally carries its meaning -- so the word she failed on becomes the word that frees her.

questions.stem: Why does the writer include the final paragraph, which begins 'I learned a great many new words that day'?

options.text: To sum up the day and close on the writer's new happiness
To introduce a brand-new character for the first time
To describe the weather outside the well-house
To argue that the teacher had made a mistake
To begin a completely different adventure

questions.explanation: The last paragraph gathers up the day's learning and ends with the 'happier child' longing for a new day -- a rounding-off.

questions.stem: In 'I tried vainly to put them together', what does 'vainly' mean here?

options.text: Very proudly
Very quickly
Looking in a mirror
Without success
With great skill

questions.explanation: She 'tried vainly' -- her attempt to fit the pieces together failed, so 'vainly' means without success.

questions.stem: Why do the writer's eyes fill with tears when she picks up the doll's pieces near the end?

options.text: She is afraid her teacher will punish her
She is tired after the long walk home
She has hurt her hand on a sharp fragment
She now understands and feels sorry for what she did before
She wishes she could go back outside

questions.explanation: The passage links the tears to realising 'what I had done' and feeling 'repentance and sorrow' for the first time -- new understanding brings regret.

questions.stem: Which four words does the writer say she knows were among the new ones she learned that day?

options.text: Pin, hat, cup, doll
Sit, stand, walk, run
Mother, father, sister, teacher
Light, hope, joy, life
Water, mug, doll, spout

questions.explanation: She writes: 'I do know that mother, father, sister, teacher were among them'.

questions.stem: Which phrase from the passage is a simile?

options.text: like Aaron's rod, with flowers
the cool stream gushed over one hand
the motions of her fingers
I dashed it upon the floor
I felt my way to the hearth

questions.explanation: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'. 'like Aaron's rod, with flowers' uses 'like' to compare the blossoming world to the flowering rod.

questions.stem: By calling this 'that eventful day', how does the writer want the reader to view the day looking back?

options.text: As an ordinary day much like any other
As a day she would rather forget
As a day that was mostly wasted
As a turning point that mattered enormously in her life
As a day full of dull, repeated lessons

questions.explanation: 'Eventful', paired with 'happier child' and longing for a new day, frames the day as a momentous turning point in memory.

questions.stem: What does 'somehow the mystery of language was revealed to me' suggest happened at the pump?

options.text: She was told a secret by the person drawing water
She learned to read a book for the first time
She began to speak aloud in full sentences
She suddenly grasped that things have names that words stand for
She discovered where the water in the pump came from

questions.explanation: The 'mystery of language' being 'revealed' marks the moment she understood that the spelled word stood for the thing -- names for things.

questions.stem: Which best describes the overall shape of the whole passage?

options.text: It lists facts about a house in no particular order
It moves from confusion, through a moment of discovery, to happiness
It compares two different children throughout
It repeats the same event several times over
It argues for and against learning to spell

questions.explanation: The passage travels from muddled, uncomprehending spelling, through the pump's revelation, to the joyful, hopeful close -- confusion to discovery to happiness.
